$comment: Trans Afrique — a journey series, not a category. Afrinkong's signature product and deliberately outside the eight experiences: an experience is a lens you look at the continent through, and this is a month of somebody's life. In the grid it would have been a ninth tile in a row of eight.
$why_here: AFRICA ISN'T ONE PLACE is the first thing the homepage says. Trans Afrique is that sentence as a product — the physical expression of it. Most operators say come to our country; this says come and cross the continent.
$pricing: These are journey prices and NOT the daily rate multiplied out. The ground journey in tourism/rates.json is priced per vehicle per day — $450 Private, $650 Signature, $1,000 Bespoke — and that is the right shape for a week or two. An expedition is not: twenty-one days at the Bespoke rate would be $21,000 against a band that tops out at $12,000, and the difference is real rather than a discount. Length earns it. One vehicle and one driver committed for a month cost less per day than the same pair for four days, the coordination is written once and used for thirty days instead of seven, and a route that repeats across departures is a route already solved. So the bands are stated as bands, per journey, and the file says why.
$what_it_buys: Not kilometres. Multiple countries, landscapes, cuisines and cultures inside one itinerary the traveller did not have to assemble — plus the parts that are genuinely hard from abroad: border coordination, permits, park arrangements, accommodation chosen rather than searched for, and somebody reachable when a plan fails at a frontier post on a Sunday.
name: Trans Afrique
line: Don’t just cross Africa. Experience it with a team.
sub: One continent. Many countries. One extraordinary journey.
say: From the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean. From rainforest to savanna. From ancient kingdoms to modern cities. Cross Africa one country at a time, by road, through the places that cannot be understood from an airport window.
$hero:
The opening spread, and it is four photographs rather than one.

A single frame can only argue one kind of crossing. Four argue the claim the headline makes: a loaded vehicle on a red road, a convoy on tarmac with people walking beside it, an elephant crossing in front of that convoy, and a camel caravan in the Horn. Same idea, four Africas — which is what 'many countries' has to look like if it is not going to be a phrase.

It rides the site's fixed-window architecture: position:fixed picture, clip-path:inset(0) band, so the photographs stand still while the title travels over them. Nothing between the band and the picture may carry transform, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, will-change or contain — each demotes the fixed to absolute and the effect dies with no error. The cross-fade is opacity ONLY, which makes a stacking context and not a containing block, so it is the one animation this element can safely have. docs/window-band.md is the full account.

Every slide is in the DOM, so with scripting off or animation refused the reader still gets the first frame and every alt text.

hero.alt: A loaded four-wheel drive with a roof box driving away on a red laterite road, dust rising behind it, the road running on over green hills towards a line of higher country on the horizon
hero.sub: One continent. Many countries. One extraordinary journey.

$door:
The homepage band, and it is a title sequence rather than a paragraph. The old version told a morning in the second person and ended on a button; it was warm, and it made the reader work out for themselves what was being sold. This states the proposition first and names the product afterwards, which is the order a film uses — cold open, then title card. The eyebrow says 'series' and not 'Trans Afrique' precisely so that the name still has somewhere to land.

The copy lives here rather than in index.html because the door and the page are one product and were drifting apart: the band said one thing about a crossing and /trans-afrique said another, and nothing made them agree. The three facts are not written here at all — they are derived from the levels and the routes, so a new crossing or a changed length cannot leave a stale number on the homepage.

door.line: Cross Africa. Don’t just visit it.
door.lede: Some journeys are measured in countries. Others are measured in everything that happens between them.
door.sub: Multi-country journeys by road, with the people, expertise and support to make the crossing possible.

$idea: The frame between the door and the machinery. Somebody arriving from the homepage has been sold a morning and nothing else; sending them straight into six support domains and three price bands asks them to evaluate a product they have not yet been told the shape of. This is the paragraph that says what a crossing is, and it is the only place on the site where the argument is made in distances rather than in adjectives.

idea.title: The idea
idea.line: Africa is too large to be a destination.
say: Dakar to Mombasa is further than Lisbon to Kabul, and there are fifty-four countries in between. A week in one of them is a week in one of them — which is the right journey for most people most of the time, and it is what the rest of this site is for.
idea.tail: Nobody assembles that from home. Borders keep their own hours, permits are booked in months rather than days, and the part that decides whether a month works is having somebody whose job is the phone call at the frontier post on a Sunday.

$levels: Three ways to travel the same continent, and the difference is who designed the route. Private is yours; Signature is ours and you pick the dates; Expedition is a fixed departure with a fixed number of seats, which is the only one of the three where scarcity is a fact rather than a technique.

levels.name: Trans Afrique Private
levels.say: Your route, your dates, your length. A private vehicle and a dedicated driver-host for the whole crossing, and an itinerary written from the beginning rather than chosen from a list.
levels.who: For travellers who know roughly what they want the year to look like.

levels.name: Trans Afrique Signature
levels.line: The route is ours. The dates are yours.
levels.say: One of the crossings below, designed and driven before, run privately for your party on the dates you choose.
levels.who: For travellers who want the thinking done and the journey still theirs.

levels.name: Trans Afrique Expedition
levels.line: A fixed departure, and a fixed number of seats.
levels.say: A set itinerary, a set date and a small group who travel it together. Twelve travellers, eight countries, thirty-four days, one journey across Africa.
levels.who: For travellers who would rather join a crossing than commission one.

$routes: Every country named is one the atlas already carries, so a crossing cannot promise a border the rest of the site has never written up. The strands under each are the lenses that route actually leads on.

routes.name: Trans Afrique — East
routes.say: Rift lakes, two gorilla forests and the migration, overland and in that order.
routes.shape: Nairobi to Arusha, the long way round.

routes.name: Trans Afrique — West
routes.say: Six countries down the Atlantic, and the food changes at every border.

routes.name: Trans Afrique — South
routes.say: Desert to delta to the falls, across five borders and most of a continent’s weather.

routes.name: Trans Afrique — The Continental Expedition
routes.say: Nine countries, top to bottom, in one continuous crossing. Cross borders, follow ancient roads, enter the wilderness, meet the people, see the places — and travel with a team built for the journey.

$included: Split the same way the rest of the site splits money: what Afrinkong earns, and what Africa costs. Keeping accommodation on the arranged side rather than the included side is deliberate — it is arranged and it is charged, and calling it included would make the band a fiction.
included: Private ground transport for the whole crossing
A driver-host, and specialists along the route
Journey coordination from arrival to departure
24/7 support while you are on the road
arranged: Accommodation, chosen rather than searched for
Domestic flights where a leg is better flown
excluded: Your own meals and personal expenses
fine: Bands are the Afrinkong journey fee — what we earn for building and running the crossing. Accommodation, park fees, permits and domestic flights are arranged by us and passed through at cost; international flights, visas, insurance and your own meals are yours. Every crossing is quoted as a whole, in writing, before anything is held.
motto: Some journeys need a guide. Trans Afrique needs a team.
$support: Six domains rather than twelve job titles. A list of people — doctor, nurse, driver, historian, chef — reads as staffing; naming what is covered reads as capability, and it is also the more honest shape, because which individual travels changes with the route while what has to be covered does not. It keeps the medical line from making this sound like a medical tour, which is the thing a long expedition with a doctor on it can easily start to sound like.
support_say: Not every journey needs every specialist. The route determines the team — and the team is assembled per crossing, not kept on a bus.

support.name: Medical
support.say: Where the itinerary, the group size and the destination call for it.

support.name: Mobility
support.say: The vehicles, the roads, the borders and what to do when one of them closes.

support.name: Security
support.say: Assessed per route and per season, and arranged locally and lawfully or not at all.

support.name: Cultural
support.say: People who can tell you what you are looking at, in the language it is spoken in.

support.name: Wildlife and nature
support.say: Trackers and naturalists for the stretches where that is the point.

support.name: Journey operations
roles: Chef or culinary specialist on selected expeditions
support.say: The person whose whole job is that the month works, and the ones who record it.

$medical: Written to be exactly true and no more. An accompanying medical professional is support in addition to insurance and local emergency services, never a substitute for either, and the site says so in the same breath as the offer rather than in a footnote somebody has to go looking for. Insurance stays mandatory — it is already the one requirement rates.json marks as hard.

medical.title: When the route demands more
medical.say: On selected crossings a medical professional accompanies the expedition. The level of support is set by the itinerary, the group size, the route and the conditions — and it is confirmed for your crossing before you book.
medical.but: It is expedition support in addition to travel and medical insurance and to local emergency services, never in place of either. Every traveller carries their own cover, and that requirement does not change because a doctor is on the crossing.
medical.alt: Eight expedition vehicles drawn up together on an open pan, people standing between them, an empty plain running to the horizon behind

$close: The page used to end like an article — a sentence and a link. An expedition company ends with a way in, and with two of them because the two audiences are genuinely different: somebody who wants a crossing designed around them, and somebody who wants to be told which of ours fits. One button for each, and neither of them is a checkout.

close.title: Ready to cross?
close.say: Tell us how you want to travel, how long you have and what you want to be changed by. We will say which crossing fits, and what it costs, in writing before anything is held.
close.alt: A woman leaning out of a moving vehicle's window smiling at the camera, dry hills and grassland running away behind her
close.line: Where do you want Africa to take you?

$map: Its own section, and the page's signature. Each crossing takes a colour and its own line; East and South are drawn over the Continental spine they are segments of, narrower and on top, so the overlap reads as what it is rather than as a collision. The legend names every country, which is the question the map raises and a legend of counts would leave unanswered.
$short: The one-word name each crossing goes by in the homepage door's row of four. Derived string surgery on the full name gave 'The Continental Expedition', which is twice the width of its three neighbours and unbalances a row that exists to be scanned. Written down rather than computed, because it is an editorial decision about what a crossing is called when there is room for one word.
$photography: Uploads, resized to 1600w and 800w and renamed for what is in the frame, which is the standing rule of images/uploads. The originals are 2 to 3.5 MB each and several are 5,000 pixels wide; a hero that ships four of those is a hero nobody on a phone ever sees.
$philosophy: The turn, lifted out of the idea section and put on a photograph. It was a pull quote between two paragraphs, which is the right place for a sentence and the wrong place for the page's thesis. On a road with people walking beside it, 'you move through it' stops being a phrase and becomes a description of the frame.

philosophy.pull: You don’t visit Africa. You move through it.
philosophy.say: A crossing is the other answer. You travel by road, you wake up in a different country most weeks, and the continent changes slowly enough to watch it happen: the landscape first, then the language, then what is for sale at the roadside, then what is for dinner.
philosophy.alt: A convoy of expedition vehicles on a tarmac road at dusk, seen from inside one of them, with a family walking along the verge under acacia trees

$pages: Trans Afrique is a series inside Afrinkong, not a single landing page, and this is the copy for each page of it. One page was trying to do the work of nine: desire, philosophy, trust, choice, geography, four itineraries, price and invitation, stacked, so the reader met the medical protocol before they had decided they wanted a crossing at all. Split, each page answers one question and hands the reader the next one. Nothing was cut — every block that was on the long page is on one of these, at more length than it had.
